title: Seven times a day (ch. 16)
hook: the monks pray seven times a day, as the psalm says
tomorrow: Nothing before the work of God (ch. 43)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ladder of humility: rungs you climb by stepping down, with love at the top. Your line was down is up. Where did you take the lower place? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

"Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." That's a line from a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, the hundred and eighteenth by its numbering. A poet writing about how much he loves God's law. It reads like a figure of speech, the way someone says they've told you a thousand times. Saint Benedict didn't read it as a figure of speech. He read it as a schedule. In chapter sixteen of his Rule, he takes the psalm at its word and builds the whole monastery's day on it. Today: the Divine Office.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY I HAVE GIVEN PRAISE.` → `A FIGURE OF SPEECH?` → `BENEDICT READS A SCHEDULE.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen is short and practical. The prophet says seven times a day, Benedict writes, and we keep that sacred number if we pray at these hours: Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers and Compline. Lauds at dawn, Vespers toward evening, Compline before sleep, and the others spaced through the working day. Then he notices that the same psalm also speaks of rising at midnight to give praise. So the monks rise in the night, too, for the night office. Two lines from one psalm, and the whole day and night is mapped. That arrangement of prayer has a name: the Divine Office. The monks don't wait until they feel like praying. The bell rings, they gather, and they pray mostly the psalms, aloud, together, verse answering verse across the choir. What does it do to a day? A day without anchors tends to run in one long blur from alarm to pillow. A day with set hours of prayer is cut into pieces, like a field divided by hedges, and God is at every gate. Nobody in the choir has to invent the words; the psalms supply them. And when a monk is tired or distracted, the hour comes anyway and carries him. The Church still prays the hours today, now usually called the Liturgy of the Hours. Priests and religious pray it, and lay Catholics are invited to join, at home, on the bus, with a book or an app. The seven times are still there in the psalm, waiting to be taken at their word.
screen: `THE PSALM SAYS SEVEN. BENEDICT SAYS WHEN.` · `AND AT MIDNIGHT, THE NIGHT OFFICE.` · `A DUTY, SUNG MOSTLY IN PSALMS.` · `THE DAY CUT INTO PIECES BY PRAYER.` · then, large: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray at three set times today. Settle, and breathe. Look at the shape of the day ahead and choose three anchors. One near waking. One somewhere in the middle, maybe a lunch break. One near sleep. Picture each one clearly: where you'll be, what you'll see. At each anchor, all you need is a minute. If you pray, you can say a line from a psalm, or the Our Father, or simply stop and turn toward God. If you don't, you can stop and take three slow breaths and notice where you are. Fix the three times now, so they arrive without being chased. The bell holds the time.
Divine Office. The set hours of prayer through the day and night, mostly psalms, prayed as a duty and a gift. Today's word.
Your line: seven times a day. Today, keep your three anchors. When each one comes, stop, even if it's in the middle of something. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

fork.setup: you're Benedict. your psalm says seven times a day I praise you, and also, I rose at midnight to praise you. how do you set the monastery's day?
options: seven hours of prayer by day, and rising at night as well.
one long prayer at dawn that counts for all seven.
seven times in total, with one of them at midnight.
fork.reveal: Benedict keeps both lines: seven day hours, from Lauds to Compline, and the night office besides.

original.note: Latin, the words of the psalm Benedict quotes: seven times a day.
